The Surah of Noah, peace be upon him, is Meccan, and its verses number twenty-eight.

﴿Indeed We sent Noah to his people: "Warn your people"﴾. That is, "by warning them." Here "أنْ" is a verbal particle (maṣdariyyah, a particle that turns the following verb into a verbal noun), and the preposition governing it has been omitted, so the verb is connected to it directly. Omitting the preposition before both أنَّ and أنْ is common practice. The clause that follows it is an imperative, as in His saying, ﴿and that you set your face﴾ (10:105). The reason is that what matters for connecting the particle to a verb is that the verb form signifies the verbal noun, and this does not differ between a declarative and an imperative form. The requirement that the relative clause of a noun-relative (al-mawsul al-ismi) be declarative exists only so that definite nouns can be described by declarative sentences. The harf-relative (al-mawsul al-harfi) is not like that. Since the declarative and the imperative are equal in signifying the verbal noun, they are equal in being valid as a connecting clause. Each of them is then stripped of the particular meaning of its form, and the bare event remains, free of the meanings of command, prohibition, past, and future. It is as if it were said: "We sent him with warning." It has also been said that the meaning is: "We sent him, saying to him: Warn," that is, "We sent him with the command to warn." It is also permissible for "أنْ" to be explanatory (mufassirah), explaining the sense of saying contained in "sending," in which case the clause has no place in the grammatical structure (i'rab). On the first view, its place is in the accusative (naṣb) according to Sibawayh and al-Farra', and in the genitive (jarr) according to al-Khalil and al-Kisa'i, as is well known. It is also read as "أنْذِرْ" without "أنْ," on the understanding that the verb of saying is intended.

﴿before a painful punishment comes upon them﴾, whether swift or delayed, so that they may have no excuse whatsoever.

ۤ﻿"He said" — this is a resumptive clause, built upon a question arising from the narration of his being sent, with the aforementioned manner. It is as if it were said: "What did he (peace be upon him) do?" So it was said: "He said to them:"

﴿O my people, indeed I am a clear warner to you﴾ — one who warns, making clear the reality of the matter. And His, exalted is He, saying:
Verse 3 of Surah Nuh, as quoted in the commentary: ﴿That worship Allah, fear Him, and obey me﴾. It is connected to "a warner" (nadhir) according to both of the two aspects mentioned above.

"He will forgive you some of your sins" — that is, some of your sins, namely what has passed in the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance), for Islam erases it (yajubbu-hu).

﴿And will defer you to a specified term﴾ — this is the furthest limit (al-amad al-aqsa) which God Most High has decreed for them on the condition of faith and obedience, beyond what He has decreed for them should they remain in disbelief and disobedience. For the description of the term as "specified" (musamman), and the linking of their deferment to it with faith and obedience, is clear evidence that they have another term, which they will not exceed if they do not believe. This is what is meant by His words, Most High: ﴿Indeed, the term of God﴾, that is, what He has decreed for you on the assumption that you remain in disbelief.

﴿When it comes﴾ while you are still in the disbelief you are in.

﴿Cannot be deferred﴾ so hasten to Me with faith and obedience before its coming, lest its condition, which is your remaining in disbelief, be fulfilled and so it comes, and the condition for deferment to the specified term be fulfilled so that you are deferred to it. It is also permissible that what is meant by it is the time of the coming of the punishment mentioned in His words, Most High: "before a painful punishment comes upon them," for that is a term fixed for it definitively. Taking it to mean the longer term is not supported by the context. How could it be otherwise, since the sentence is a reason (ta'lil) for the command to worship, which entails forgiveness and deferment to the specified term? Thus what is negated at the coming of the term must be the promised deferment, so how can it be conceived that what is supposed to come is the specified term itself?

﴿If only you knew﴾ — that is, if only you knew anything, you would hasten to what I have commanded you.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 5:

﴿He said﴾: i.e., Nuh (upon him be peace), conversing with his Lord and reporting to Him, the Exalted, and He knows best his state, what passed between him and his people of talk and counter-talk over those long periods, after he had exerted the utmost effort in the call, gone beyond every known limit in warning, and his stratagems had been exhausted and his excuses had failed him.

﴿My Lord, indeed I have called my people﴾ to faith and obedience.

﴿by night and by day﴾: i.e., constantly, without slackening or delay.

I need to translate this passage from Abu al-Su'ud's commentary.

"﴿So my calling them did not increase them except in flight﴾ — fleeing from what I called them to. The attribution of the increase to the calling is because it is its cause, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿it increased them in faith﴾."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 7:

﴿And indeed, whenever I call them﴾ to faith.

﴿so that You may forgive them﴾ because of it.

﴿they put their fingers in their ears﴾ i.e., they stopped up their hearing so as not to listen to the call.

﴿and wrapped themselves in their garments﴾ i.e., they went to excess in covering themselves with them, as if they wanted their garments to cover them, or to cover them so that they would not see, out of their aversion to looking at him, or so that he would not recognize them and call them.

﴿And they persisted﴾ i.e., they devoted themselves to disbelief and sins. It is a metaphor taken from when a donkey turns its ears toward the herd of wild asses and advances upon them.

﴿and were arrogant﴾ toward following me and obeying me, ﴿with great arrogance﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verses 8–9:

﴿Then indeed I called them openly.﴾ ﴿Then indeed I proclaimed to them and I spoke to them in private, a private speaking.﴾ That is: my calling them was at one time after another, and once after another, in various modes and differing methods. And "thumma" (then) indicates the difference between the modes, for open proclamation is stronger than private speech, and combining the two is more severe than doing either alone. Or it indicates the delay of some of them after others. "Jihaaran" (openly) is in the accusative governed by "da'awtuhum" (I called them) as a verbal noun (masdar), since it is one of the two types of calling. Or "da'awtuhum" is taken to mean "jaahartuhum" (I addressed them openly). Or it is an adjective of an implied verbal noun, meaning: I called them a calling that was open, i.e., openly declared. Or it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: openly declaring.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verses 8–9:

﴿Then indeed I called them openly.﴾ ﴿Then indeed I proclaimed to them and I spoke to them in private, a private speaking.﴾ That is: my calling them was at one time after another, and once after another, in various modes and differing methods. And "thumma" (then) indicates the difference between the modes, for open proclamation is stronger than private speech, and combining the two is more severe than doing either alone. Or it indicates the delay of some of them after others. "Jihaaran" (openly) is in the accusative governed by "da'awtuhum" (I called them) as a verbal noun (masdar), since it is one of the two types of calling. Or "da'awtuhum" is taken to mean "jaahartuhum" (I addressed them openly). Or it is an adjective of an implied verbal noun, meaning: I called them a calling that was open, i.e., openly declared. Or it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: openly declaring.

ۦ﴿So I said: "Seek forgiveness from your Lord"﴾ by repenting from disbelief and sins.

﴿Indeed He is ever Forgiving﴾ to those who repent. It is as if they made excuses and said: "If we are upon the truth, how can we abandon it? And if we are upon falsehood, how would He accept us after we have devoted ourselves to it for a long time?" So he commanded them with what erases the sins that had preceded from them and brings them benefits. For this reason, He promised them what would have greater effect on their hearts and what they would love more than immediate worldly gains. It was also said: when they denied him after the repeated calling, Allah, exalted is He, withheld rain from them and made the wombs of their women barren for forty years, and it was said seventy years. So He promised them that if they believed, Allah would grant them abundance and remove from them what they were in.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 11:

﴿He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾ i.e., abundant in its pouring. The intended meaning of "the sky" (al-sama') is either the canopy (al-mizallah) or the clouds (al-sahab).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 12:

﴿And He will provide you with wealth and sons, and will make for you gardens﴾ (jannat), meaning orchards.

﴿And will make for you﴾ in them.

﴿Rivers﴾ (anhar), meaning flowing ones.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 13:

﴿What is the matter with you that you do not hope for dignity from Allah?﴾ This is a denial that there should be any cause for them, in their not hoping for Allah, the Exalted, to have dignity (waqar), taking "hope" (al-raja') in the sense of "belief" (al-i'tiqad). The phrase "la tarjuna" (you do not hope) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the addressees, and its governing element (al-'amil) is the meaning of stability (al-istiqrar) contained in "lakum" (for you). This is on the basis that the denial is directed only at the cause, while the content of the circumstantial clause is established, not at both together, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And why should I not worship the One who originated me?﴾ The phrase "lillah" (for Allah) is connected to an implied element (mudmar) and stands as a circumstantial clause (hal) from "waqaran" (dignity). Had it been placed after it, it would have been a qualifier (sifah) of it. The meaning is: what cause has arisen for you, while you are not believing in Allah, the Exalted, in a greatness that necessitates glorifying Him through faith in Him and obedience to Him?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 14:

﴿And indeed He has created you in stages.﴾ That is: while the state you are in is utterly contrary to what you are upon, namely that you know that He, exalted is He, created you in successive stages: first as elements (ʿanasir), then as nourishment, then as humours (akhlat), then as drops of sperm (nutfah), then as a clinging clot (ʿalaqah), then as a lump of flesh (mudghah), then as bones and flesh; then He brought you into being as another creation. For falling short in revering One whose affairs are these, in overpowering might and complete beneficence, while knowing this, is something that scarcely issues from a rational person. It has also been said: al-rajaʾ here means al-amal (hope), so the meaning is: "What is the matter with you that you do not hope for Allah to have reverence (tawqir)," that is, glorification, for one who worships Him and obeys Him, and you are not in a state in which you hope for Allah, exalted is He, to glorify you in the abode of reward. And "lillah" is an explanation of what is revered (al-muwaqqar). Had it been placed later, it would have been a complement to waqar (dignity). The first reading is the one demanded by the eloquence of the revelation, for it is fitting for the condition of the disbelievers that it be deemed remote that they do not believe in the dignity of Allah, exalted is He, and His greatness, while they witness its signs and its judgements, which necessarily necessitate belief. As for their not hoping for Allah to glorify them in the abode of reward, this is not in the realm of what is deemed remote or denied. Moreover, making waqar mean tawqir is forced; and in His saying "lillah" as an explanation of what is revered, if it were placed later as a complement to waqar, there would be contradiction that is not hidden, for its being an explanation of the one who reveres requires that the reverence originate from Him, exalted is He, while waqar being an attribute of the addressees, and its being a complement to waqar would necessitate that waqar be an attribute of Him, exalted is He. It has also been said: "What is the matter with you that you do not fear Allah's greatness and power to seize you with punishment?" That is: what excuse do you have for abandoning fear of Him, exalted is He?

And it is narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "What is the matter with you that you do not fear Allah's punishment, nor hope from Him for reward." And from Mujahid and al-Dahhak: "What is the matter with you that you do not care for Allah's greatness." Qutrub said: it is a Hijazi dialect; they say "lam arju," meaning "lam ubali" (I did not care). And His exalted saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 15:

﴿Have you not seen how Allah created seven heavens in layers?﴾ That is: corresponding to one another, one above the other.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 16:

﴿And He made the moon therein a light﴾, i.e., illuminating the face of the earth in the darkness of the night. Its attribution to all of them (the heavens), although it is in the lowest heaven, is because the lowest heaven is enveloped by all the other heavens, so what is in it is [considered] to be in all of them. Or it is because each one of them is transparent, not blocking what is behind it, so that all of them are seen as if they were one heaven; and it necessarily follows from this that what is in one of them is as if it were in all of them.

﴿And He made the sun a lamp﴾, which removes the darkness of the night, and by its light the people of the world see the face of the earth and witness the horizons, just as the people of a house see by the light of a lamp what they need to see. The moon is not in this position; rather, it is a light only in a general sense.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 17:

﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth, a growth﴾ — i.e., He brought you into being from it. The verb "caused to grow" (inbat) is used metaphorically for "brought into being" (insha'), because it is more indicative of coming into existence and formation from the earth. As for "nabatan" (a growth), it is either a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing "anbatakum" with the augmenting letters removed, and it is called an ism masdar (a noun functioning as a verbal noun); or it denotes what results from the action, i.e., "He caused you to grow from the earth, so you grew as a growth." It is also permissible that the original form was "anbatakum min al-ard inbatan, fa-nabatum nabatan," in which case the verbal noun is omitted from the first clause and the verb from the second, each being satisfied by what is mentioned in the other, as was discussed earlier in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah touches you with adversity, there is none to remove it but Him; and if He intends for you good, there is none to repel His bounty﴾.

[Verse 71:18] ﴿Then He will return you into it﴾ by burial at your death, ﴿and bring you forth﴾ from it at the Resurrection and the Gathering.

﴿A bringing forth﴾, certain, with no doubt about it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 19:

﴿And Allah has made the earth for you a spread-out carpet﴾, that you may move about upon it as you move about upon your rugs in your houses.

And the placing of "for you" (lakum) between the "making" (al-ja'l, the act of making) and its two objects, although its proper place is after them, is due to what has passed many times: the concern to clarify that what is made is among their benefits, and the arousing of eagerness for what is deferred. For the soul, when something that ought to be put first is delayed, especially when the fronted element hints that it is one of the benefits, remains awaiting it, so that when it arrives the soul is settled in it with especially firm settlement. (p-40)

Verse 20 of Surah 71 (Nuh): ﴿So that you may traverse from it roads, wide highways.﴾ That is, broad paths. It is the plural of fajj, which is a wide road. It was also said: it is a passage between two mountains. The phrase "min" (from) is connected to what precedes it, because of the sense of "taking" (ittikhadh) contained in it; or it is connected to an implied verb, and it is a circumstantial clause (hal) of subulan (roads), meaning: "existing from the earth." Had it been placed after it, it would have been a qualifying adjective (sifah) for it.

Noah said: "My Lord, they have disobeyed me." The wording of the narration is repeated because of the long time since the narration of his private supplication to his Lord; that is, he said, addressing Him, may He be exalted.

"My Lord, they have disobeyed me": that is, they persisted in disobeying me regarding what I commanded them, even though I exerted myself in guiding them with admonition and reminder.

"And they have followed one whose wealth and children add to him nothing but loss": that is, they continued to follow their leaders, whom their wealth had made arrogant and whose children had deceived them. This became a cause for an increase in their loss in the Hereafter, so they became exemplars for them in loss. In describing them this way there is an indication that they followed them only because of the standing those leaders had gained through wealth and children, and not because of any doubt they had observed in them that would in general justify following them. It is also read as (wuldu) with a ḍammah and sukūn, as a dialectal form like ḥuzn, or as a plural like asad.

**﴿And they schemed﴾** — coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon the relative clause of "man" (those who); the plural is used in view of its meaning, just as the singular in the earlier pronouns is used in view of its wording.

**﴿a great scheme﴾** — i.e., great to the utmost degree. It has been read with the lighter form (*kubār*, with taShdīd omitted; the reading is *kubbāran* in the heavier form and *kubāran* in the lighter). The first (the heavier form, *kubbāran*) is more emphatic than the second. The heavier form is more emphatic than *kabīr* (great). This is their scheming in religion, their barring of people from it, and their inciting of them against the harming of Nuh, peace be upon him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 23:

﴿And they said: Do not leave your gods.﴾ That is: do not abandon their worship at all in favor of the worship of the Lord of Noah.

﴿Nor leave Wadd, nor Suwa', nor Yaghuth, nor Ya'uq, nor Nasr.﴾ That is: and do not give up the worship of these. They singled them out for mention although they are included in what preceded, because they were the greatest of their idols and the most important to them. These idols later passed from them to the Arabs: Wadd belonged to the tribe of Kalb, Suwa' to Hamdan, Yaghuth to Madhhij, Ya'uq to Murad, and Nasr to Himyar. It is also said that these were names of righteous men who lived between Adam and Noah. It is said further that they were children of Adam (peace be upon him); when they died, Iblis said to those who came after them: "If you were to make their images, you would look at them and seek blessing through them." They did so, and when those (men) died, he said to those who came after them: "They used to worship them," and so they worshipped them. It is also said that Wadd was in the form of a man, Suwa' in the form of a woman, Yaghuth in the form of a lion, Ya'uq in the form of a horse, and Nasr in the form of a vulture. It is also read (Wuddan) with a damma on the waw, and (Yaghuthan wa-Ya'uqan) for the sake of harmony. Their diptotic inflection is withheld because of foreignness (ʿujma) and proper-name status (ʿalamiyya).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 24:

﴿And they have led many astray.﴾ That is: the leaders (al-Ru'asa').

﴿Many﴾: a great multitude of people. Or it refers to the idols, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿My Lord, they have indeed led many of the people astray﴾ and ﴿Do not increase the wrongdoers except in error.﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿataf) upon His saying, exalted is He: ﴿My Lord, they have disobeyed me﴾, in the sense of relating the speech of Nuh after "qala" (he said) and after the conjunction (waw) that substitutes for it. That is: he said, "My Lord, they have disobeyed me," and he said, "Do not increase the wrongdoers except in error." He placed the explicit noun in the position of their pronoun, to record upon them excessive wrongdoing and to give the reason for the supplication against them. What is sought is error in the arrangement of their deceit and the welfare of their worldly affairs, or perdition and ruin, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness﴾. This is supported by his supplication against them, upon him be prayer and peace, that will come later.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 25:

﴿Because of their sins﴾ i.e., on account of their sins. The "mā" here is an extra (zā'idah) particle placed between the preposition and the noun, for emphasis and magnification. Whoever does not regard it as extra makes it a noun (nakirah) and takes "khaṭī'ātihim" (their sins) as an apposition (badal) to it. It is also read as "mimmā khaṭāyāhum" and "wa-mimmā khaṭāyātihim," meaning: because of their sins, those counted and others besides them.

﴿They were drowned﴾ by the Flood, not by any other cause.

﴿And were made to enter a Fire﴾ The intended meaning is either the punishment of the grave, which follows the drowning, even though they were in the water. From al-Ḍaḥḥāk: they were drowned on one side and burned on the other. Or it is the punishment of Jahannam, and the word "then" (ta'qīb, sequence) is used because it is treated as following their drowning, given its nearness and its certain occurrence without doubt. The indefiniteness of "fire" (nār) is either to glorify and terrify it, or because God, may He be exalted, prepared for them, according to their sins, a particular kind of fire.

﴿And they found for themselves no helpers besides God﴾ i.e., none of them found a single helper. This contains an allusion to their taking gods besides God, and that these are unable to help them, and it contains a mockery of them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 26:

﴿And Noah said: "My Lord, leave not upon the earth any dweller from among the disbelievers."﴾ It is conjoined (ʿatf) to its like preceding it. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Because of their sins﴾ ... etc. is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) placed between his supplication, upon him be peace, against them. It serves to inform from the very beginning that what befell them of drowning and burning did not befall them except because of their sins, which Noah, upon him be peace, enumerated, and it points to their deserving destruction on account of them. It is not that it is a narration of the drowning and burning themselves, in the manner of narrating what passed between him, upon him be peace, and them of circumstances and statements; for otherwise it would have been delayed until after the narration of this supplication of his. And "dayyaran" (a dweller) is among the nouns used in general negation; it is said: "There is not a dweller (dayyar) in the house," or "dayyur," like qayyam and qayyum, meaning: anyone. It is on the pattern fa'al (fayʿal) from al-dawr, or from al-dar, its original form being dayʿwar, which has undergone what happened to the original of sayyid, in comparison with af'āl (plural forms); otherwise it would have been dawwaran.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 27:

﴿Indeed, if You leave them﴾ (that is, leave them, all of them or some of them, upon the earth),

﴿they will mislead Your servants﴾ (away from the path of truth),

﴿and they will not beget except a wicked disbeliever﴾. That is: only one who will become wicked and disbelieving. He described them by what they will come to be, and it is as if this is a justification against an objection that might be raised: that the supplication for their total destruction is made while there is the possibility that among their descendants there might be one who believes. He said it only because of the firm certainty of his knowledge of what will happen from them and from their offspring after he had tested them and surveyed their conditions for close to a thousand years.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 71, verse 28:

﴿My Lord, forgive me (p-42) and my parents﴾. His father was Lamak ibn Mattushalakh (Lamech son of Methuselah), and his mother was Shamkha bint Anush (Shamkha daughter of Enosh). They were both believers. It is also said that they were Adam and Hawwa' (Eve). It was recited as (وَلِوَلَدَيَّ) "and my two sons", meaning Sam and Ham.

﴿And whoever enters my house﴾: that is, my dwelling. It is also said: my mosque. It is also said: my ship.

﴿Believing﴾: by this condition, his wife and his son Kan'an (Canaan) were excluded. However, the blessings and peace of God be upon him did not definitively determine their exclusion until it was said to him that "he is not of your family", and its details have passed in surah Hud.

﴿And for the believing men and the believing women﴾: he generalized the supplication to them after singling out those connected to him by lineage and religion.

﴿And do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction﴾: that is, in ruin. It is said that their children also drowned with them, but not as a punishment for the children, rather to intensify the torment of their fathers and mothers, since they wished for the destruction of their children, who were dearer to them than their own souls. The blessings and peace of God be upon him said: "They were destroyed in one destruction, and they departed to various destinies." It is reported from al-Hasan that when he was asked about this, he said: "God knew their innocence, so He destroyed them without punishment." It is also said: God made the wombs of their women barren and dried up the loins of their fathers forty or seventy years before the Flood, so that there was no child with them when they drowned.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah Nuh will be among the believers whom the supplication of Nuh, peace be upon him, will reach."
